'''''Gelidium''''' is a genus of [[thalloid]] [[red algae]] comprising 134 species. Its members are known by a number of common names.<ref group=note>Recorded common names are tengusa, makusa, genso, niu mau tsai, japansche scheleiachtige mos, steen-or klipbloem, hay tsay, olus marinus, sajur laut, tschintschau, tschoo-hoae, onikusa, hirakusa, obusa, rødalge-slaegt, gelídeos, punalevä-suku, tokoroten, kanten, tokoro-tengusa, kinukusa, isingglass, hai-ten-gusa, tocoroten, tengusa-agar, limu lo-loa, hai-tengusa, onigusa, oyakusa, kanten weed, goumaocai, hime tengusa, shihua and tanmae.</ref>

== Description and life cycle ==
Specimens can reach around {{convert|2-40|cm|abbr=on|sigfig=2}} in size. Branching is irregular, or occurs in rows on either side of the main stem.  ''Gelidium'' produces [[tetraspore]]s.  Many of the algae in this genus are used to make [[agar]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Tronchin|first1=E. M.|last2=Freshwater|first2=D. W.|last3=Bolton|first3=J. J.|last4=Anderson|first4=R. J.|year=2002|title=A Reassessment and Reclassification of Species in the Genera Onikusa Akatsuka and Suhria J. Agardh ex Endlicher (Gelidiales, Rhodophyta) Based on Molecular and Morphological Data|journal=Botanica Marina|volume=45|issue=6|pages=548–558|doi=10.1515/BOT.2002.058|s2cid=84425094}}</ref> [[Agarocolloids]] are known to be extracted in algae belonging to the orders [[Gracilariales]] and [[Gelidiales]] with certain applications in the food and cosmetics. Gelling properties often differ among species, seasons, seaweed age, and substitutions between sulphate esters, among other compounds.  Sulphate composition often dictates gel strength, while methyl esters determine gelling and elasticity.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last1=Mouradi-Givernaud |first1=Aziza |last2=Amina Hassani |first2=Lalla |last3=Givernaud |first3=Thierry |last4=Lemoine |first4=Yves |last5=Benharbet |first5=Oumaima |date=1999-04-01 |title=Biology and agar composition of Gelidium sesquipedale harvested along the Atlantic coast of Morocco |journal=Hydrobiologia |language=en |volume=398 |pages=391–395 |doi=10.1023/A:1017094231494 |issn=1573-5117 |s2cid=23800143}}</ref>

''Gelidium'' is assumed to follow the ''[[Polysiphonia]]'' life cycle, with sexual and tetrasporangial generations.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Melo |first1=Ricardo A. |last2=Neushul |first2=Michael |date=1993 |editor-last=Chapman |editor-first=A. R. O. |editor2-last=Brown |editor2-first=M. T. |editor3-last=Lahaye |editor3-first=M. |title=Life history and reproductive potential of the agarophyte Gelidium robustum in California |url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-94-011-1998-6_27 |journal=Fourteenth International Seaweed Symposium |series=Developments in Hydrobiology |language=en |location=Dordrecht |publisher=Springer Netherlands |pages=223–229 |doi=10.1007/978-94-011-1998-6_27 |isbn=978-94-011-1998-6|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Tetrasporangia formation is also known to be affected by temperature and other environmental factors including light, salinity and moisture,<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Santelices |first1=Bernabe |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HlLq4x6WDn8C&dq=santelices+1988+gelidium&pg=PA1 |title=Synopsis of Biological Data on the Seaweed Genera Gelidium and Pterocladia (Rhodophyta) |last2=G |first2=Bernabé Santelices |date=1988 |publisher=Food & Agriculture Org. |isbn=978-92-5-102717-2 |language=en}}</ref> although germination rates remain unaffected based on an earlier study.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Correa |first1=J. |last2=Avila |first2=M. |last3=Santelices |first3=B. |date=1985-03-01 |title=Effects of some environmental factors on growth of sporelings in two species of Gelidium (Rhodophyta) |journal=Aquaculture |language=en |volume=44 |issue=3 |pages=221–227 |doi=10.1016/0044-8486(85)90246-7 |issn=0044-8486}}</ref>

In 1993'', Gelidium robustum'' in Santa Barbara, California was investigated for 16-months showing tetrasporangial abundance throughout the year, but may not have the ability to germinate despite maximum spore output.<ref name=":2" />

== Distribution ==
''Gelidium'' are widely distributed globally, specifically in tropical to temperate regions, but lacking in polar regions.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal|last=Santelices|first=B.|date=1991|editor-last=Juanes|editor-first=J. A.|editor2-last=Santelices|editor2-first=B.|editor3-last=McLachlan|editor3-first=J. Reports of ''G. pussillum'' occurrence outside of its specified range may be questionable and requires further verification.<ref name=":0" />

== Ecology ==
Gelidiales consists of many species that are economically important as they produce agar while some serve ecologically significant functions such as substrate cover.<ref name=":6" /> The growth of ''Gelidium'' can primarily be affected by nutrient availability and light. In turn, these factors are also regulated by temperature and water movement, respectively. Santelices (1991) evaluated how eight factors may affect ''Gelidium'' productivity, all of which are important in understanding how different interactions correlate to production yield. Some of these factors include seasonality, phenotypic characters, age, reproductive state, and even the source of the algae.<ref name=":6" />

==Historical environmental analysis==
''Gelidium'' species have been collected, pressed and maintained in [[Herbarium|herbaria]] and personal collections from the 1850s onwards since seaweed collecting became a popular pastime for the middle classes as well as scientists in Europe and North America.<ref name="Giaimo2016">{{cite web |last1=Giaimo |first1=Cara |title=The Forgotten Victorian Craze for Collecting Seaweed |url=https://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/the-forgotten-victorian-craze-for-collecting-seaweed |website=Atlas Obscura |access-date=27 October 2020}}</ref> These numerous well-documented specimens can provide information beyond taxonomy.<ref name="Trethewey2020">{{cite web |last1=Trethewey |first1=Laura |title=What Victorian-era seaweed pressings reveal about our changing seas |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2020/oct/27/what-victorian-era-seaweed-pressings-reveal-about-our-changing-seas |website=The Guardian |access-date=27 October 2020}}</ref>

Sensitive measurement of stable nitrogen isotope ratios in ''Gelidium'' species collected in southern Monterey Bay between 1878 and 2018 showed a pattern of changes that matched with changes in the [[California Current|California current]] and provided support for a theory about the end of the local fishing industry.<ref name="Miller_etal_2020">{{cite journal |last1=Miller |first1=Emily A |last2=Lisin |first2=Susan E |last3=Smith |first3=Celia M |last4=Van Houtan |first4=Kyle S |title=Herbaria macroalgae as a proxy for historical upwelling trends in Central California |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society B |date=2020 |volume=287 |issue=1929 |article-number=20200732 |doi=10.1098/rspb.2020.0732|pmid=32546101 | pmc=7329038  |doi-access=free }}</ref> [[Isotopic signature#Nitrogen isotopes|Nitrogen isotope ratios]] are well established as a measure of nutrient productivity in aquatic ecosystems. The California current runs along coastal California and correlation with information on fish catches indicates that an increase in nutrient-rich cold water is important for fish productivity, notably sardines.<ref name="Ware&Thompson1992">{{cite journal |last1=Ware |first1=D M |last2=Thompson |first2=R E |title=Link between longterm variability in upwelling and fish production in the northeast Pacific Ocean |journal=Can. J. Fish. Aquat. Sci. |date=1991 |volume=48 |issue=12 |pages=2296–2306 |doi=10.1139/f91-270 |url=https://cdnsciencepub.com/doi/10.1139/f91-270 |access-date=27 October 2020|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The California current has only been measured since 1946. The correlations with the ''Gelidium'' nitrogen ratios allowed the California current to be projected back into the nineteenth century and compared with historical records of fish catches.<ref name="Miller_etal_2020" /> The data matched, notably for the highest sardine catches through the 1930s and then the sudden decrease from 1945 to 1950 that ended the Monterey cannery industry. This information supports the theory that environmental changes as well as overfishing caused the collapse of the local fishery business. More broadly, this suggests that elemental analysis of historical samples of macroalgae can provide evidence of primary productivity processes. The species used included specimens of ''G. coulteri'', ''G. robustum'', ''G. purpurascens'', ''G. pusillum'' and ''G. arborescens'' collected over a 140-year timespan from the 6 km coastline between Point Pinos, [[Pacific Grove, California|Pacific Grove]] and [[Cannery Row]], Monterey in California, US.<ref name="Miller_etal_2020" />

== Taxonomy and nomenclature ==
Gelidiaceae has 159 species, considered to be the largest family in Gelidiales with four major genera: ''Capreolia, Gelidium, Gelidiophycus,'' and ''Ptilophora.''<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=JAMAS |first1=MAYRA |last2=IHA |first2=CINTIA |last3=C. OLIVEIRA |first3=MARIANA |last4=M. P. B. GUIMARÃES |first4=SILVIA |last5=T. FUJII |first5=MUTUE |date=2017-07-25 |title=Morphological and molecular studies on Gelidiaceae and Gelidiellaceae (Gelidiales, Rhodophyta) from Brazil with description of the new species Gelidium calidum |journal=Phytotaxa |volume=314 |issue=2 |page=195 |doi=10.11646/phytotaxa.314.2.2 |issn=1179-3163}}</ref>

''Gelidium'' was first described by [[Jean Vincent Félix Lamouroux|Lamouroux]] in 1813 and is regarded to be one the genera with the most species. Species diversity has been established by previous studies, whereas, molecular analysis reveals biogeographic relations that concerns its current distribution pattern in oceans.<ref name=":0" />

Identification of species has been a challenge as sexual plants are somewhat difficult to find in nature, therefore, other physiological features are examined instead, such as branching patterns and vegetative traits, but subsequent studies revealed that these are also affected by its development and environmental factors<ref name=":1" /> highlighting the need for genetic studies utilizing genetic markers.<ref name=":0" />
